summary: Automatic host fencing slice 3: every ready host reads every other host's fence device every few minutes without powering anything off — the management controller's own report of which machine it manages, and that machine's power state — and reports the results to the pool master over a new pool-mTLS peer route. The master keeps them in memory, overlays a per-method fence readiness on the membership it reports, and never writes them into its durable record, so a settled pool's signed authority does not move because a check ran. A result the master has not had confirmed for three intervals is stale, and a stale check is never readiness. The Hosts tab gains a Fencing column that replaces the fence text and row clutter, the pool gains a 'ready for N of M hosts' line, and promotion names the method each blocking host would be shut out with and warns advisorily from the candidate's own last check. It also closes slice 2's verified-open review findings: the master's withdrawal decision is projected and drives the row's actions instead of the host's echo, a host's local BMC record no longer outlives the pool it was made in, PoolHostBMC.observed_at's meaning is settled in the contract and the guide, the orphaned pending password script is retired, a manual profile wins over a withdrawn automatic one, the latent advertise drop is fixed, the reinstall-after-half-configure case is documented, the Clear fence device button no longer opens an empty Set BMC access form, and the inert generation assertion is replaced by a byte-identical durable-record assertion. Independent review rejected the first round: a member holds no other host’s fence credential on disk, so only the master could complete a check and the master — the one host the feature exists for — was permanently reported "Not protected". A member now unseals the target’s credential from its own signed replica in memory for the pass and discards it, and the IPMI power read takes the password through the environment exactly as the identity read does; nothing materialises another host’s fence password on a member. Every result is bound to the profile it was taken against, so a replaced device cannot inherit the old one’s success; the pool count is computed by Core on the master over the pool’s ready hosts and only displayed by the UI; a pool of one host reports its own honest state instead of a permanent "not checked yet"; the pass runs on its own worker so it cannot delay the storage-cluster reconcile; and the documentation no longer claims readiness gates a promotion, which it never did. API impact: changed contract, implemented both sides.

guide.reason: The Hosts tab gains a column operators read to answer 'could this host be shut out if it were lost', so docs/guide/pool-authority-and-recovery.md gains 'The Fencing column': that the hosts check each other's management controllers every few minutes and that no check can power anything off, a table of every state the column can show (ready with the number of confirming hosts, a lab virsh device, stale, each failing reason naming the host that found it, no device, a deliberate withdrawal, not checked yet, a pool master too old to report, and a pool master that is not reporting) with what to do about each, what the 'What each host found' disclosure holds, the pool's 'ready for N of M hosts' line, and that a restarted master or a rebuilt Controller honestly reports 'not checked yet' for one interval. The withdrawal row of the existing state table now says the row shows the master's decision immediately, including for a host that is switched off, and that a hand-typed device recorded afterwards wins; the name-conflict row gains the reinstall-after-a-half-finished-pass case an independent review raised. The promotion steps say the verdict names the method each host would be shut out with and that the check warning under it is advisory and decides nothing. docs/guide/README.md follows. Round two adds the single-host row (no other host to check from, and a single-host pool needs no fence device at all), the replaced-device row, an explicit statement that these checks decide nothing and the promotion is decided by the live fence, and removes the claim that a host which is not fence-ready cannot be promoted over.

api.reason: New peer route POST /api/v1/pool/fence-checks (pool mTLS, member → master): PoolFenceCheckRequest{checks: [PoolFenceCheck{host_id, result, detail, power}]}, at most 64 entries and 64 KiB. The member certificate identifies the caller, the report is credited to it, and an entry naming the caller itself is dropped — a host does not get to say whether it can be shut out. result is a closed set (ok, unreachable, credentials_rejected, identity_mismatch, certificate_changed, tool_missing, no_profile, unusable); 400 for an invalid body, 401 for a peer that is not an admitted ready member, 405 with Allow: POST, 409 from a host that is not the master. A member talking to a master too old to serve the route gets 404 and simply keeps its own results; nothing is retried in a way that matters, because the next pass replaces them. PoolMember gains fence_readiness (PoolFenceReadiness{ready, methods:[PoolFenceMethod{kind, state, reason, checks}]}), a memory-only observation the master overlays on the membership it reports, exactly as replica_generation already is, and never part of the durable record — so an older Core simply omits it and a Controller shows 'not reported', never ready. PoolPromotionHost gains fence_kind and the advisory fence_check_warning. PoolHostBMC.observed_at is now documented as 'when this finding last changed', which is what it has meant since slice 2 stopped re-reporting unchanged findings; freshness for fencing comes from PoolFenceCheck.observed_at, stamped by the master's own clock, with stale set after three check intervals. The Controller's members projection gains fence.readiness and fence.provisioning_disabled, the latter being the master's own withdrawal decision that the row's actions are now driven from rather than the host's echo of it. Both sides are implemented; the Controller relays and displays only and stores nothing. docs/api/*.json and the generated reference are updated, generate_api.py --check passes and tests/test_api_contract.py (74 tests) passes. Round two of this slice, after independent review: PoolFenceCheck gains profile, a 16-hex stamp over the recorded kind, address, target, account, pinned certificate and cipher plus the hardware identity, which the master compares against what its membership records now and drops every result that does not match — so replacing a fence device reads as not checked yet instead of inheriting the previous device's success. PoolFenceMethod.state gains no_peer for a pool with no other host to be checked from, which is not a wait. PoolFenceReadiness gains pool (PoolFenceSummary{ready, total, unready}), the master's own count over this pool's ready hosts, carried on the pool master's own row: an ejected tombstone and a host that has not finished joining are neither counted nor named, and a client displays the number rather than adding up the rows it renders. The contract now states plainly that readiness gates nothing — a promotion is decided by PoolFenceUsable and the live fence proof, exactly as before this slice.

roadmap.reason: The published roadmap describes shipped capability at a coarser grain than one fencing slice; the plan records this slice's status and what it settled.

state.reason: Every fence device, identity and provisioning decision stays in the pool master's durable membership record, unchanged by this slice. The checks this slice adds are Core observations the master holds in memory and reports; the Controller relays and displays them and keeps nothing.
state.record: The durable record is unchanged: the pool master's pool-peer.json membership holds PoolMember.fence, system_uuid, bmc and bmc_provisioning_disabled, and the fence material lives in the Core fence-credential store and replicates sealed inside each member's signed authority replica. The check results and the readiness derived from them are deliberately NOT durable: the master keeps them in process memory keyed by the host that reported them, overlays them on the membership copy it reports as PoolMember.fence_readiness, and re-establishes them within one check interval (five minutes) after a restart, reporting every method as 'unknown — not checked yet' honestly in the meantime. That is the reason no new durable store exists: nothing here is a decision, and a durable copy of it would be a second source of truth for something the hosts re-derive by looking. A fresh Controller recovers readiness the same way it recovers everything else, from inventory.managed.membership reported by the master, after at most one interval. This slice also adds poolPeerState.LocalBMC.PoolID on each host, so a host that leaves a pool keeps the evidence that the nexfence account on its own controller is its own (without which the leftover account would be a permanent conflict) while nothing the old pool decided survives with it. A member never holds another host's fence material on disk: it unseals the copy inside its own signed authority replica in memory for one pass and discards it, so a read-only check does not spread every host's fence password across the pool.

verification.method: Go unit tests in internal/vmhost against fake Redfish endpoints (httptest TLS pinned to the server's own certificate) and a fake ipmitool/fence-agent command runner, and in internal/agent against a two-host in-process pool lab over the real mutual-TLS peer transport with real in-band provisioning and a stubbed controller read; React unit tests (node --test src/*.test.mjs) and npx tsc --noEmit; a real-browser review of the Fencing column against mocked API data; python3 scripts/generate_api.py --check; python3 scripts/check_docs.py --worktree; python3 -m unittest discover -s tests. RESULTS, all run in this working tree on 2026-09-22: go build ./... PASS; go vet ./internal/... PASS; go test ./internal/... PASS (all packages); npx tsc --noEmit PASS; every web/src/*.test.mjs PASS; python3 scripts/generate_api.py --check PASS; python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py' PASS (394 tests, including test_api_contract.py's 74 and the repository-privacy suite); python3 scripts/check_docs.py --worktree PASS. BROWSER REVIEW: the real pool-members module was bundled with the project's own esbuild into an untracked local scratch directory (never web/dist) and driven in headless Chromium through Playwright against fixture reports covering ready, stale, unreachable, credentials-rejected wording, no device, operator-withdrawn, not-checked-yet, a pool master too old to report readiness, a pool master that is not reporting, an empty pool, and the loading and error states PoolMembers renders itself. Captures were inspected: the column header is a real th, every state's text carries the meaning with the badge colour only repeating it, the 'What each host found' disclosure opens from the keyboard alone and lists each checking host with when it was last confirmed, no console error was raised, and the loading and error strings are the host's own. TWO DEFECTS WERE FOUND AND FIXED, then re-captured: a pinned 64-character certificate fingerprint overflowed the constrained column (fixed with overflow-wrap and an explicit column width), and the not-reporting master's reason was printed twice in the same cell (the column now leaves that sentence to the fence-device line). NOT-DESTRUCTIVE PROOF: TestAContinuousCheckCannotPowerAnythingOff asserts structurally that a whole checking pass sends no non-GET Redfish request and runs no fence agent with anything but --action=status. NO-CHURN PROOF: TestManyCheckingPassesMoveNothingDurable runs twenty full passes on both hosts of a real two-host lab and asserts the authority generation, the authority digest and the master's pool-peer.json bytes are all unchanged afterwards, while readiness is still reported; the same byte-identity assertion replaced the inert generation assertion an independent review identified in slice 2's unchanged-report test. ROUND TWO, after independent review found ten items: every one is fixed, and the three load-bearing ones were each verified to fail with their fix reverted — TestAMemberChecksTheMastersControllerWithTheCredentialItsReplicaCarries reproduces the reviewer's own demonstration exactly ("this host holds no fence credential for that management controller (from member-1)") when the secret is read from the store instead of the replica; TestRemovingTheAccountRetiresThePasswordItOpened and TestAnUnchangedControllerReportDoesNotSwallowAnOriginChange each fail with their slice-2 fix reverted. New tests: the member->master credential path with nothing stubbed but the controllers themselves (a fake ipmitool that records every invocation and its environment, asserting the password never enters argv and only mc guid and chassis power status are ever issued); a whole pass over an IPMI device, a Redfish httptest server and a laboratory virsh device asserting only GETs, only reads and no fence agent at all; the profile-stamp drop on a replaced device; the single-host no_peer state; and the pool count ignoring an ejected host. The lab stub was narrowed so it fails the test if a check ever runs with no credential, which is what let the gap hide. RESULTS round two: go build, go vet, go test -count=1 ./internal/... all PASS; go test -race -count=1 ./internal/agent/ PASS (25 s); npx tsc --noEmit and every web suite PASS; generate_api.py --check PASS; check_docs.py --worktree PASS; the tests/ suite PASS. BROWSER REVIEW round two added the promotion verdict with an ok, a failing and a stale proving host, and a pool of one host; captures inspected: the advisory renders as two emphasis lines inside the table cell (computed style: no padding, no border, no background) rather than the block callout .warning draws, and it says "Advisory:" and "this stops nothing" in the UI and not only in the guide.
untested: No physical management controller has been contacted and no host has been powered off, in this slice or in the two before it. Every Redfish interaction is against an httptest server and every ipmitool interaction against a fake command runner, so what real firmware does under a check every five minutes from every other host in a pool — session-table exhaustion in particular — is unproven. The cadence, the one-target-at-a-time pass and the bounded timeouts are chosen to avoid it, not measured against hardware.

The IPMI power read is a second short RMCP+ session per target per pass, because ipmitool cannot issue Get System GUID and a chassis power status in one invocation. Two short sequential sessions every five minutes is not a session storm, but it is twice what Redfish needs and it has not been measured on real firmware.

The staleness bound (three check intervals, so about fifteen minutes) and the five-minute interval with a fifth of jitter are judgements, not measurements. They are package variables and a test drives them directly rather than waiting.

Controller replacement is proven only at the level this slice owns: the master's reported membership carries readiness, and a master that has forgotten its checks reports them as unknown and re-establishes them in one pass (TestARestartedMasterReportsNotCheckedYetRatherThanReady). A whole Controller was not rebuilt against a live lab pool in this slice.

The browser review used mocked API data in a fixture page, not a running Controller against real hosts. It proves the column's rendering, wording, keyboard behaviour and states; it does not prove the projection end to end, which the Go and contract tests cover separately.

Watchdog fencing is not built. PoolFenceReadiness is a list of methods so a second one can be added without a contract change. There is no watchdog code and no watchdog placeholder: round two removed the one map entry in the UI that named a kind no Core can produce.

Unsealing a member's replicated credential runs the same private script the store would hold, from standard input rather than from a file. That is the same content and the same trust as the on-disk path, but it does mean a check executes a script that arrived in the replica; the replica is signed by the pool CA and its credentials are sealed to that member, which is what makes it the same trust as everything else in it.
